title: Functional Programming in Mainstream Languages
summary: Grounding this whole group in reality: why pure FP languages stayed niche while their idioms went mainstream everywhere, how Java, Python, JavaScript, and Kotlin each borrowed them, and how to mix FP with OOP without wrecking a team's readability.

slides.markdown:
This closing topic in the group is the reality check: every idea covered so far — pure functions, higher-order functions, closures, ADTs, monads, laziness — showed up in a **mainstream, mostly-OOP language** near you, usually years after a pure FP language proved the idea out.

Haskell stayed a research and niche-industry language. Lambdas, Streams, comprehensions, and Optional showed up in Java, Python, and JavaScript instead — the *idioms* went mainstream even though the *languages* that pioneered them mostly didn't.

This topic ties the whole group to real, everyday code: which language borrowed which idiom, what a data pipeline looks like in each style, and the honest failure mode of pushing FP style onto a codebase or team that isn't ready for it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the idioms won and the languages didn't
slides.markdown:
Haskell, Erlang, and Scheme proved out purity, laziness, and immutability decades ago, yet none became a top mainstream language, while `map`/`filter`, lambdas, and `Optional` are now everywhere. The gap has a consistent explanation: an **idiom** is adoptable one call site at a time; a **language switch** is not.

A team can start using `Optional` instead of `null` in new code today, incrementally, without touching anything else. Switching the whole codebase to Haskell requires rehiring, retraining, and rewriting — a cost most organizations never accept, no matter how compelling the ideas are.

So mainstream languages did the pragmatic thing: they absorbed the *idioms* that paid for themselves without demanding the full paradigm shift — lambdas without mandatory purity, `Optional` without mandatory pattern-match exhaustiveness everywhere, Streams without a lazy-by-default runtime. Purity, laziness by default, and true tail-call guarantees stayed rare, precisely because those three specifically require whole-language, whole-ecosystem commitment to pay off — you can't bolt them onto 20% of a codebase the way you can bolt on a `map` call.

Java 8 (2014) is the clearest single case of an OOP language deliberately absorbing FP idioms wholesale, decades into its life. Two additions did the work: **lambdas** (first-class function values, closing the gap the [higher-order-functions topic](higher-order-functions-and-composition) described for pre-Java-8 code) and the **Streams API** (`map`/`filter`/`collect` as a fluent pipeline over a collection).

`orders.stream().filter(o -> o.getStatus() == COMPLETED).map(Order::getAmount).reduce(0.0, Double::sum)` reads as a named pipeline over a collection — filter to completed orders, extract amounts, sum them — using the exact `map`/`filter`/`reduce` vocabulary from earlier in this group, expressed with Java's `Comparator`/`Function`/`Predicate` interfaces underneath.

What Java deliberately did **not** adopt: purity enforcement (a lambda can still mutate captured state), immutability by default (collections stay mutable unless you wrap them), or laziness by default (Streams are lazy internally between intermediate operations, but that's an implementation detail, not a language-wide guarantee). It borrowed the useful vocabulary, not the whole paradigm.

Python never marketed itself as functional, but a meaningful slice of idiomatic Python code is FP in disguise:

- **Comprehensions** — `[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]` is `map` and `filter` fused into one readable expression; it's the idiomatic Python way to write what other languages spell as a `.map().filter()` chain.
- **`functools`** — `reduce`, `partial`, and `lru_cache` (memoization as a one-line decorator) are direct, named imports of the exact FP concepts covered earlier in this group.
- **Generator expressions** — `(x for x in huge_file)` is Python's opt-in lazy evaluation, covered in the previous topic, built into the core syntax rather than a library add-on.

What's notably absent: Python has no enforced immutability (lists and dicts are mutable by default; `tuple` and `frozenset` are opt-in), and no tail-call optimization at all — a deliberate design choice, since deep tail-recursive Python code will `RecursionError` regardless of how it's written, exactly as the recursion topic in this group covers.

slides.sectionTitle: Imperative-OOP vs. FP style, side by side
slides.markdown:
The same task — extract, filter, and total a collection of records — rendered in the two competing styles this whole group has been building toward.

![An imperative loop with a mutable accumulator compared with a filter-map-reduce functional pipeline for the same task](assets/loop-vs-pipeline.svg)

Neither panel is "more correct" — they compute the identical result. The imperative panel's mutable accumulator is visible and traceable one line at a time; the functional panel names each transformation stage as an independent, reusable, testable unit. Which one reads better depends on the language's idioms and the team's habits, which is exactly what the next few slides get into.

assets.alt: An imperative loop with a mutable accumulator compared with a filter-map-reduce functional pipeline for the same task

slides.markdown:
JavaScript had first-class functions and array methods baked into the language from early on, which is why FP-style code has always felt native there, without a Java-8-style deliberate addition:

```javascript
const total = orders
  .filter(o => o.status === "completed")
  .map(o => o.amount)
  .reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0);
```

This chain uses exactly `filter`/`map`/`reduce` as built-in `Array.prototype` methods — no import, no library, no special syntax beyond arrow functions (themselves added in ES6 mainly to make passing lambdas around less verbose than the older `function` keyword). Combined with closures being fundamental to how JavaScript's callback-heavy style works at all (event handlers, Promise chains, `setTimeout`), it's fair to say JavaScript absorbed more of FP's *day-to-day mechanics* by default than Java did — while still keeping mutable objects, `this`-binding quirks, and no purity enforcement, so it's every bit as much a pragmatic hybrid as the others, just with a different starting point.

slides.sectionTitle: Kotlin and Scala: multi-paradigm by design
slides.markdown:
Kotlin and Scala represent a different strategy from Java's "bolt FP idioms onto an existing OOP language": both were **designed from the start** to be multi-paradigm, with FP idioms as first-class citizens alongside full OOP interop, not an afterthought layered on top.

Kotlin's `sealed class` plus `when` gives you the exhaustive-matching ADT pattern from earlier in this group with real compiler-enforced exhaustiveness — not an approximation via `instanceof` — while classes, interfaces, and inheritance work exactly as in Java, and the two styles interoperate freely within the same file, even the same function.

Scala goes further: it runs on the JVM and interoperates directly with Java libraries and classes, while also offering genuine pattern matching, immutable-by-default `case class`es, and a much richer type system with first-class support for the functor/monad vocabulary from earlier in this group (`for`-comprehensions are literally sugar over `flatMap`/`map`). The practical upshot for both: you get to choose FP or OOP per problem, per function, without switching languages or fighting the compiler either way.

slides.sectionTitle: Forcing FP style onto a team that isn't ready
slides.markdown:
The failure mode this topic exists to warn about: adopting FP idioms as a blanket team mandate — "no more for-loops," "everything must be a pipeline" — faster than the team's shared vocabulary and debugging habits can absorb it.

The concrete symptoms show up in code review and incident response, not in a style guide: a five-stage `.map().filter().reduce()` chain that a teammate unfamiliar with functional idioms has to mentally simulate line by line, slower than they'd read an equivalent loop; a production stack trace through deeply composed lambdas that shows generic framework frames instead of the business logic that actually failed (the same debuggability cost the composition topic covered, now multiplied across a whole team instead of one function); and PRs that take longer to review because the reviewer is learning the pattern *and* checking correctness simultaneously.

The fix isn't abandoning FP idioms — it's introducing them where they clearly win (a genuinely multi-stage transformation, a `null`-safety-critical `Optional` chain) and leaving simple, single-purpose logic as plain loops and conditionals, paced with the team's actual familiarity rather than a blanket style mandate handed down all at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Refactoring an imperative method into a Streams pipeline

slides.markdown:
Every topic in this group compounds into the same practical skill: recognizing when a mainstream language's borrowed FP idiom is the right tool, and using it without pretending you're writing Haskell.

Purity and immutability (topic 1) tell you when a function is safe to reason about in isolation. Higher-order functions and composition (topic 2) give you the pipeline vocabulary. Closures (topic 3) are the hidden mechanism making callbacks and memoization work. Recursion and TCO (topic 4) are the loop-replacement, with real caveats about which runtimes honor it. ADTs (topic 5) are how you model data so illegal states can't compile. Monads (topic 6) are how you chain fallible or async steps without a pyramid of null-checks. Laziness (topic 7) is how you defer work until it's actually needed, and the cost when that deferral piles up.

All seven show up, in borrowed form, in the Java/Python/JavaScript/Kotlin code most working engineers actually write — which is exactly why this group is interview-relevant even for someone who will never write a line of Haskell professionally.
